evidence.claim: Company stores and miners’ homes follow the valleys of coal country.

evidence.claim: The Coal Heritage Trail crosses rugged mountains and follows streams and rivers on roads that are often narrow and curving.
evidence.quote: The Coal Heritage Trail crosses rugged moun- tains and follows the path of streams and rivers and is often narrow and curvy.

evidence.claim: Small commercial districts occupy the valleys, while residential areas climb the steep mountains.
evidence.quote: Small commercial districts line the narrow valleys and modest residential areas climb the steep mountains.

evidence.claim: The Federal Highway Administration identifies this National Scenic Byway with the coal industry’s effects on the land and on society, pointing to company towns, railroad structures and reclaimed mining land along the corridor.
evidence.quote: The region commemorates the history and culture of the coal industry and the impact it has had on the physical and social environment. Numerous resources line the corridor, including coal company towns, tipples, railroad structures, and reclaimed mining lands.

evidence.claim: The Federal Highway Administration identifies this National Scenic Byway
evidence.quote: Coal Heritage Trail National Scenic Byway

evidence.claim: The West Virginia byways guide describes a two-lane highway through this industrial landscape.
evidence.quote: Accessibility: Curvaceous two-lane state and U.S. highway

evidence.claim: Mining jobs brought people from many lands into southern West Virginia.
evidence.quote: jobs brought people from many lands and all walks of life

evidence.claim: Changes in the industry later left deserted mines and remnants of company towns beside stores, clubhouses and courthouses crafted by Italian stonemasons.
evidence.quote: Transitions in the coal industry have left behind deserted mining sites and remnants of once-thriving company towns alongside the com- pany stores, club houses and courthouses crafted by Italian stone masons.

evidence.claim: The road received national scenic byway designation in 1998.
evidence.quote: Date of Designation: 1998 (national designation)

evidence.claim: At Beckley, one mine had already taken on an educational role: commercial operations ended in 1953, and the exhibition mine opened in 1962.
evidence.quote: Mine operations ceased in 1953

evidence.claim: the exhibition mine opened in 1962.
evidence.quote: The Beckley Exhibition Coal Mine opened in 1962

evidence.claim: Its restored passageways and vintage track preserve part of the working environment.
evidence.quote: It consists of 1,500 feet of restored passageways and entries with 3,000 feet of vintage track.

evidence.claim: For a southbound drive, follow the corridor from Ansted through Beckley and Mullens toward Welch.
evidence.quote: The Trail begins on RT. 52 in Bluefield and travels to Welch, the takes RT. 16 North to Ansted.

evidence.claim: from Ansted through Beckley and Mullens toward Welch.
evidence.quote: Motoring on the CHT you will pass through National Register Historic Districts in the towns of Bluefield, Bramwell, Welch, Mullens and Beckley.

evidence.claim: Itmann lies between Mullens and Pineville, off WV 16.
evidence.quote: between Pineville and Mullens off  West Virginia Route 16.

evidence.claim: At Welch, the trail changes to US 52 for the journey toward Bluefield.
evidence.quote: The Trail begins on RT. 52 in Bluefield and travels to Welch, the takes RT. 16 North to Ansted.

evidence.claim: Bramwell, beside the Bluestone River, is connected by US 52 to Bluefield to the south.
evidence.quote: U.S. Route 52 passes through the eastern part of Bramwell, connecting the town with Bluefield to the south

evidence.claim: Valley commercial districts sit below residential areas climbing the steep mountains.
evidence.quote: Small commercial districts line the narrow valleys and modest residential areas climb the steep mountains.

evidence.claim: Itmann’s company store and office forms a sandstone complex arranged around an open courtyard.
evidence.quote: It is a Classical Revival style complex built of native sandstone.  It consists of four sections (A through D) laid out in an open courtyard plan.

evidence.claim: Architect Alex B. Mahood designed the building, constructed in 1923–1925 to serve the mining community.
evidence.quote: It was designed by architect Alex B. Mahood and built in 1923–1925.

evidence.claim: constructed in 1923–1925 to serve the mining community.
evidence.quote: It was built as a company store for the local mining community.

evidence.claim: The complex has four sections, including a one-story loggia, with taller gabled sections flanking the courtyard.
evidence.quote: It consists of four sections (A through D) laid out in an open courtyard plan.

evidence.claim: including a one-story loggia, with taller gabled sections flanking the courtyard.
evidence.quote: Sections A and C are 2+1⁄2-story parapeted gable front sections located on the northern and southern sides of the courtyard and Section D is a 1-story parapeted half gable roofed loggia.

evidence.claim: The town preceded it: Pocahontas Fuel Company built 120 dwellings near Barkers Creek in 1916 and opened the mine in 1918.
evidence.quote: In 1916, the Pocahontas Fuel Company constructed 120 dwellings near the mouth of Barkers Creek. The Itmann mine was opened in 1918 by the Pocahontas Fuel Co.

evidence.claim: Its name compresses the company president’s initials and surname, I. T. Mann.
evidence.quote: Isaac T. Mann, or I. T. Mann which was eventually shortened down to Itmann.

evidence.claim: The store survives, but the town account describes it as empty after part of it served as a homeless shelter.
evidence.quote: Half of the company store was used as a homeless shelter while the other half was unused. Now it is empty.

evidence.claim: The store survives
evidence.quote: The Itmann Company Store and Office is still standing

evidence.claim: Kimball is the site of the first war memorial building erected in memory of African-American veterans of World War I.
evidence.quote: Kimball is the site of the first war memorial building erected in memory of the African-American veterans of World War I.

evidence.claim: The town incorporated in 1911 and took its name from railroad official Frederick J. Kimball.
evidence.quote: Kimball was incorporated in 1911 and named for Frederick J. Kimball, a railroad official.

evidence.claim: It lies on the Norfolk Southern network, formerly the Norfolk and Western.
evidence.quote: The town is on the Norfolk Southern Railway (former Norfolk and Western) network.

evidence.claim: Large houses built by wealthy coal operators distinguish Bramwell on the Bluestone River.
evidence.quote: Numerous large homes were built in the town by wealthy coal operators.

evidence.claim: Large houses built by wealthy coal operators distinguish Bramwell on the Bluestone River.
evidence.quote: Bramwell is situated along the Bluestone River

evidence.claim: Coal camps multiplied in the surrounding region during the 1880s, and the town was established in 1888.
evidence.quote: In the 1880s the region around Bramwell began to rapidly grow as a coal mining center with several coal camps operating in the area. The town of Bramwell was officially established in 1888

evidence.claim: The town’s prosperity did not spare its downtown from a major fire in January 1910, when 21 buildings burned.
evidence.quote: On January 7, 1910, part of the downtown area was destroyed by a major fire. Twenty-one buildings were burned to the ground.

evidence.claim: Many houses have early-twentieth-century designs.
evidence.quote: Many of the houses are early 20th century in design.

evidence.claim: A local museum concentrates on coal and railroad history, two subjects central to the local account.
evidence.quote: There is a museum largely devoted to the local coal and train history of the area.

evidence.claim: The town entered the National Register of Historic Places in 1984. US 52 passes through its eastern side, with Pinnacle Rock State Park just southeast.
evidence.quote: In 1984, the town was named to the National Register of Historic Places by the U.S. Department of the Interior.

evidence.claim: US 52 passes through its eastern side, with Pinnacle Rock State Park just southeast.
evidence.quote: U.S. Route 52 passes through the eastern part of Bramwell

evidence.claim: US 52 passes through its eastern side, with Pinnacle Rock State Park just southeast.
evidence.quote: Pinnacle Rock State Park lies just southeast of Bramwell.
